task4_student.v316: You can no longer destroy your own program by naming it as the output. sutram hello.sm hello.sm used to compile, write the binary over your source, and say Siddh. Now it refuses (E_NIRGAM_NIVESH), your file stays as it was. An output that cannot be opened is an error now (E_NIRGAM_PATRA) instead of a false Siddh
task4_student.v317_v318_v319: A loop that builds a fresh kosh or mala every pass no longer eats memory and time. The program's output is identical; what changes is that 800,000 passes of a one-element kosh go from 37,516 KB resident to 16-20 KB, and the loop from 5 ms to 0.9 ms per 200,000 passes (per the v319 handoff's measurements). A student notices it only if their program was slow or ran out of memory before
task4_student.v320: A mala or nirmmita taken after a block no longer reads the block's old data (a new mala m[8] used to read 77 in its first and last number). A student notices it only in the rare program that was reading stale data, a bug they probably did not know they had
task4_student.v321: If you type a curly quote, an en-dash, $, @, an apostrophe, a no-break space, or an emoji, you now get an error at the character: file, line, column, the character and its code point, the line with a caret under it, and a hint ('use "', 'use -'). Before, the character vanished silently and 5 <en dash> 2 compiled and printed 5
task4_student.v322: Four new errors you will hit instead of silent wrong answers, and one fixed one. krama/agrim outside a loop are refused (E_AVARTAN_VINA); likha of a whole mala is refused (E_MALA_LIKHA, it used to print the address); a bare kosh as a condition is refused (E_KOSH_SATYA, every kosh, even an empty one, used to be true); a bad mala length is refused (E_MALA_PARIMAN, mala m[-3] used to crash). And a prakriya that ends without nivartanam now returns 0 instead of whatever the last instruction left (it used to return 15 for f(5))
task4_student.v323: You can read text. vartani_grahan() reads a whole line as a string, the first way to read text at all (grahan() only reads numbers, and hello gave 0). nivesha_anta() tells you when the input has ended, so a loop that reads every line stops at the end and not at an empty line (examples 360, 361)
task4_student.v324: You can read a file, and grahan() works properly. Example 362 reads a whole file by its path and sums its numbers; example 363 counts a file's lines by being given the file as input. grahan() now reads -5 as -5 (before: 5) and does not lose a last number with no newline after it. And because a typed -1 is now a number, grahan() sets nivesha_anta() at the end of input, so a grahan() loop should ask it
task4_student.v325: Two library answers are fixed (only if you hit those inputs): laghuttam_samapavartya no longer stops the program for a pair with 0, and brihat_ank_tak_laghu refuses a negative digit instead of returning -1. And the reference tells the truth in the rows that were false: dvaram opens and paadh reads, akshar works on bytes, the braces section, and the chakra rule in section 6a
task4_student.v326: You get a warning when a chakra has the shape of a countdown it will not make (chakra i = n tak 1 prints a Sutram suchana on stderr, the program unchanged), and a converter: vartani_tak_ank(s, ok) turns text into a number and tells you whether it was one (ok[0]), so hello is reported instead of silently becoming 0 (example 364). The books' first program now prints the size the compiler actually prints (112, not 97), the grahan() example is a whole program that adds the numbers it is given, and the 'Descending Loops' sentence is true. The paused books name the one sentence in them known to be false

worth_the_risk.v316: worth it. Risk low: 0 DIFFER; identity-based and fail-closed (an unidentifiable output is refused, not written). The only new failure mode is a refusal where the compiler used to write. It prevents the worst failure in the chain, destroying a student's source
worth_the_risk.v317_v318_v319: worth it, with the chain's biggest validation gap. Risk medium-high: ~800 lines of new codegen, a whitelist scan, frame slots, an R82 stamp; its shape is absent from the guard corpus (0 loop bodies in 788 programs contain a kosh or mala), so it rests on its gates alone. The risk is bounded the right way: the scan 'fails toward leaking', so a missed case leaks memory as before rather than corrupting anything. The payoff (37,516 KB to 16 KB) is the largest in the chain
worth_the_risk.v320: worth it. Risk medium: 38 DIFFER, every program with a mandapa changes bytes, plus a timing cost on every block exit, and one pinned program's output changed (99 to 0). It fixes a silent-wrong-data defect, the 38 DIFFER are accounted for, and the decision (zeroing over the floor) is accepted under the rule as written. Invisible to almost every student, but the defect it fixes was invisible too, and worse
worth_the_risk.v321: worth it. Risk low-medium: 0 DIFFER on the guard, but the refusal is entirely unguarded in code position (no corpus program triggers it) and the BOM carve-out is unguarded too; it rests on its 21-check gate. Silent skipping was a silent wrong answer; the diagnostic is good. The residual risk is over-refusal of a character a student legitimately uses, mitigated by the carve-out and the pack handling, neither guard-covered
worth_the_risk.v322: worth it. Risk medium: 84 DIFFER in bytes (all print and exit the same), and five behaviour changes: a program that compiled before can now refuse, and every falling-off prakriya returns a different value. Four of the five close silent-wrong or crash holes (mala m[-3] used to SIGSEGV). The fall-off change carries the most risk of the five and the least student-visible benefit (it fixes a return value nobody should have relied on)
worth_the_risk.v323: worth it. Risk low: 0 DIFFER; two new builtins, no existing program changes; the cost (>= 64 bytes per call, never given back) is documented in section 4d. The first way to read text
worth_the_risk.v324: worth it. Risk medium: 7 DIFFER; the rewrite is a hand-built macro with one computed jump, and it adds a hidden global to every grahan program. Two silent wrong answers fixed, covered by a 24-check gate
worth_the_risk.v325: worth it. Risk low: the compiler's bytes are v324's (a comment only); the library fixes are 2 and 8 lines, guard-covered through ganit (47 programs) and brihat (15); the guard tightening is pure win. The docs fixes cost nothing
worth_the_risk.v326: worth it. Risk low: the compiler change is a stderr warning only (no program's bytes change); the lib addition is a new function; the rest is docs. The warning's false-positive shape (n tak 5 warned even when it counts up) is a small cost, it warns on shape, not values

title: the eleven read as one; the guard's blind spot; the eleven descriptions; what a student gets

verdicts.task1: read as one diff, the eleven hang together. The only hard merge-order dependencies are v324 on v323 (grahan's tail needs the hidden nivesha_anta global), v318/v319 on v317 (the hoist machinery), v326's books and examples on v323, and v325's reference rows on v324 and v321, plus a validation-order dependence, in that v325 strengthened the guard (refusal diagnostics now compared) only after v321 and v322 had added the refusals it now checks. The check-first question is SAFE: v320's clearing zeroes only the scratch side [end, mark), while every hoisted kosh/mala descriptor, element, and region lives on the persistent side or in a separate 64 MiB region, so no hoisted allocation can sit inside a range a block clears, traced for the mandapa-in-a-loop shape, nested blocks, and region growth alike, and every exit path (ordinary, nivartanam, krama/agrim, prasar) rewinds through one of the two zeroing sites
verdicts.task2: the guard's blind spots are specific and counted: no loop body in any of the 788 programs contains a kosh or a mala (the hoist is guard-invisible), no corpus program triggers v321's refusal or carries a BOM, no corpus program grows a kosh past 4,097 elements or nests a mandapa past 3 depths, the warned chakra shape occurs 0 times, the FFI path is never run with --ffi, and the five new input examples were NEW and never compared against an old compiler
verdicts.task3: of the eleven descriptions, nine are accurate (v321 and v324 understated, v317/v318 accurate but incomplete), one is overstated (v319's 'anywhere', falsified by the kuru gap), and v326's 'avaroha set out' is accurate only as a question, avaroha is proposed, not built
verdicts.task4: for a student the chain lands as: text can be read, files can be read, a minus sign is read, a countdown-shaped chakra warns, a wrong character is refused at its place, and the books' sentences can be trusted, while the invisible work (the hoist's memory, the block's clearing, the output that can no longer overwrite its input) was worth doing because the defects it fixes were invisible too, and worse
